oil.summary: Crude gave back a chunk of Wednesday's geopolitical premium on Friday, with WTI settling near $89.77 (-2.63%) and Brent at $97.23 (-3.44%), yet both contracts remain up sharply on the week and month as the Middle East crisis keeps a floor under prices. The sell-off follows an intraday spike above $100 on Thursday, when Houthi strikes on two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and IRGC interceptions of three vessels in the Strait of Hormuz drove panic buying. Hormuz transits fell to their lowest since early May, and at least one Saudi tanker went dark to slip through Bab el-Mandeb. Chinese refiners have already swept up all August Kozmino loadings from Russia, reflecting a scramble to diversify away from Middle East supply. ADNOC, notably, continues to push crude tenders despite the disruption. RBOB gasoline's sharp 7.28% daily drop is an outlier worth monitoring for demand-side signals.
drivers: Strait of Hormuz near-paralysis and IRGC tanker interceptions sparked $100+ intraday spike before Friday profit-taking
Houthi strikes on Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb dark transits compound supply-route anxiety
China front-running August Russian crude allocations signals market expectation of prolonged Middle East supply disruption

gas.summary: European gas continues to outpace US benchmarks by a wide margin. TTF surged another 3.92% today to €64.325/MWh, extending a 12% weekly gain and a striking 57% monthly rally, almost certainly reflecting contagion from the Middle East shipping crisis, which threatens LNG re-routing economics and tightens Atlantic basin balances. Henry Hub, by contrast, was up a modest 1.27% to $2.953/MMBtu, remaining well below year-ago levels on a one-month basis (-8.32%), suggesting US domestic supply-demand fundamentals are not yet materially affected. On the policy front, the EU's latest sanctions package retains an exemption for Russian gas cargoes, and LNG majors are eyeing Cambodia as a new demand outlet. News flow for the US gas market today is thin; the TTF move is the dominant story.
drivers: TTF +57% on the month as Middle East shipping disruption threatens LNG route economics and tightens European supply
EU sanctions package preserves Russian gas cargo exemptions, limiting near-term European supply squeeze from that angle
Henry Hub materially lagging TTF, reflecting ample US domestic supply; spread divergence bears watching for arb flows

power.summary: EU carbon edged up 0.59% to $80.08/EUA, with a solid 6.41% weekly gain likely tracking TTF's sharp rally — higher gas prices raise the cost of gas-fired generation and support carbon permit demand as coal-switching calculus shifts. The conflict dimension is present here too: a Russian attack cut power to roughly 150,000 consumers in northern Ukraine, a reminder that the war remains an active infrastructure risk. On the strategic side, Washington is pushing small modular reactor cooperation across Southeast Asia as a counter to rising regional electricity demand. A Trump nuclear diplomacy piece flags potential complications in the Middle East nuclear sphere but the headline data supporting a deeper assessment in that direction is limited today. The electrification and AI power-demand theme also surfaced but provided no hard data to assess.
drivers: EUA gains tracking TTF's surge as higher gas costs lift marginal generation expenses and support carbon permit bids
Russian strike cuts power to ~150,000 in northern Ukraine, highlighting ongoing grid vulnerability tied to the conflict
US SMR diplomacy push in Southeast Asia signals longer-term demand-side expansion but no near-term market impact
